You extract source evidence for a paper-derived scientific benchmark. Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, with no Markdown or additional text.

Use only the fixed, line-numbered source packet. Do not use outside knowledge and do not infer an omitted coefficient, exponent, range, experimental condition, or uncertainty convention.

Extract at most one relation: the best source-supported executable quantitative relation connecting one to five numeric controls to one or two numeric readouts. A second source-reported condition is not required. Do not construct a pair, alternate world, counterfactual, task prompt, or benchmark design. If the source contains no complete relation, return {"relations":[]}.

The relation has exactly six fields: formula, parameters, controls, readouts, domain, and anchors. Formula.outputs is an executable expression tree for the source-reported central relation. Output keys must exactly match the readout names. A var leaf names a declared control and a param leaf names a declared parameter. Every declared control and parameter must occur in the formula. Numeric literals are allowed only for structural zero and one; encode every other scientific constant or fitted value as an anchored parameter. Preserve equality, approximation, fitted-relation, and asymptotic scope through the applicability statements; do not turn proportionality without its coefficient, an inequality, or an unspecified function into an exact point predictor.

A control is a numeric independent variable that can be queried within the source-supported domain. A readout is the quantitative dependent variable returned by the relation. Do not turn a latent quantity or an unreported fitted quantity into a control. Use continuous_interval only when the source supports a finite interval with minimum below maximum. Use numeric_values only for at least two explicitly supported numeric values. The domain must name every control exactly once. Record source-reported applicability or fixed context when present; otherwise use an empty applicability array.

Every formula, parameter value, control definition, readout definition, control domain, and applicability statement must carry direct inclusive source line ranges. Anchors contain line_start and line_end only. Do not generate a paraphrased support field. Use the line coordinates exactly as supplied.

Do not output source identity, schema version, an assessment, readiness flag, mechanisms, claim dependencies, ambiguity records, budget, diagnostic conditions, held-out conditions, public prose, provenance mappings, or code. Source identity and all benchmark-design fields are supplied or generated by deterministic code.

L000023	\begin{document}
L000024	
L000025	\title[aMChA quartz]{Observation of acoustic magneto-chiral anisotropy in $\alpha$-quartz}
L000026	
L000027	\author{Munkhtuguldur Altangerel}
L000028	\author{S.~Badoux}
L000029	\author{C.~Proust}
L000030	\author{D.~Vignolles}
L000031	\author{G.~L.~J.~A.~Rikken}
L000032	\affiliation{Univ. Toulouse, INSA-T, Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, LNCMI-EMFL, UPR3228, Toulouse, France.}
L000033	
L000034	\date{\today}
L000035	
L000036	\begin{abstract}
L000037	We report the experimental observation of magneto-chiral anisotropy in the longitudinal and transverse ultrasound propagation in $\alpha$-quartz. To perform such measurement, we have built an ultrasound spectrometer with unprecedented experimental resolution of the order of $\Delta v/v \sim 10^{-8}$.  We present a simple macroscopic Becquerel-like analytical model that accounts for the magnitude of the observed effect and its frequency dependence.
L000038	\end{abstract}
L000039	
L000040	\maketitle
L000041	
L000042	Chirality plays an important role in many areas of physics, chemistry and
L000043	biology, where entities exist in two non-superimposable forms (enantiomers),
L000044	one being the mirror image of the other. Chirality corresponds to an absence
L000045	of mirror symmetry and if time-reversal symmetry is also absent because of a
L000046	magnetization or an external magnetic field, an entire class of effects
L000047	called magneto-chiral anisotropy (MChA) becomes allowed. Optical MChA
L000048	corresponds to a difference in the absorption and refraction of unpolarized
L000049	light propagating through the chiral medium parallel or anti-parallel to the
L000050	field \cite{WagniereMeier,BarronVbrancich}. Initially observed in the
L000051	visible wavelength range \cite{Naturemca,kleindienst,mcaabs}, its existence
L000052	was later confirmed across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from
L000053	microwaves \cite{MicrowaveMChA} to X-rays \cite{XrayMChA}. MChA was further
L000054	generalized to other transport phenomena \cite{emchaprl}. It was
L000055	experimentally observed in the electrical transport in bismuth helices \cite
L000056	{emchaprl}, in carbon nanotubes \cite{eMChACNT}, in bulk organic conductors
L000057	\cite{Pop}, in metals \cite{Yokouchi,Aoki}, in superconductors close to the
L000058	transition temperature \cite{MChAsupercon} and in semiconductors \cite
L000059	{RikkenTe} as an electrical resistance that depends on the handedness of the
L000060	conductor and on the relative orientation of electrical current and magnetic
L000061	field. Other manifestations of MChA were observed in the propagation of
L000062	magnons \cite{MagnonMChA} and of ultrasound \cite{USMChA1,USMChA2} in chiral
L000063	magnetic crystals, and in the displacement current in chiral dielectrics
L000064	\cite{dMChA-Rikken}, further illustrating its universal character. Inverse
L000065	MChA, a longitudinal magnetization induced in a chiral medium by an
L000066	unpolarized flux, first proposed in the optical domain \cite{Theory-ioMChA},
L000067	and later for an electrical current \cite{Theory-ieMChA}, has also been
L000068	observed \cite{Exp-ieMChA}. MChA has become a prominent representative of
L000069	the wider class of non-reciprocal transport phenomena in broken-symmetry
L000070	systems, that play an important role in topological quantum systems and in
L000071	Berry phase physics \cite{Non-reciproc-review}. For a recent review of MChA,
L000072	see \cite{Review-MChA}.
L000073	
L000074	The existence of MChA in phonon transport was already predicted a long time
L000075	ago \cite{emchaprl}, but it was only more recently in magnetic crystals with
L000076	a hybridization between magnons and phonons, that the effect could be
L000077	observed as non-reciprocal ultrasound transmission close to a magnetic phase
L000078	transition \cite{USMChA1,USMChA2}. These observations are therefore better
L000079	qualified as phonon-detected MagnonMChA. Although the magnitude of the
L000080	effect was too small to be useful in phononics, this effect represents an
L000081	acoustical diode that can be inverted with a magnetic field, a highly
L000082	interesting functionality. It is therefore worthwhile to explore MChA in
L000083	phonon transport in other materials. Here we will extend the MChA family to
L000084	ultrasound propagation in diamagnetic crystals, in particular in the
L000085	archetypal chiral crystal of $\alpha$-quartz.
L000086	
L000087	For optical MChA (oMChA), a detailed quantitative microscopic theory has
L000088	been developed \cite{BarronVbrancich} and experimentally validated for
L000089	transition-metal complexes \cite{ValidationMChA}. A specific theory for
L000090	phonon MChA was developed for chiral Weyl semimetals \cite{Phonon-MChA-Weyl}
L000091	, but so far, no general prediction for diamagnetic crystals exists. For
L000092	simplicity we will consider for the remainder only the case of isotropic
L000093	media, or uniaxial media aligned with the magnetic field. Symmetry arguments
L000094	tell us that to first order the acoustic wave velocity $v$ parallel to the
L000095	magnetic field for transverse circularly polarized modes ($\pm$) and left ($L
L000096	$) or right ($D$) handed media is given by
L000097	\begin{equation}
L000098	v_{\pm }(\omega,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{B})=v(\omega)\pm \alpha^{D/L}(\omega)k\pm
L000099	\beta(\omega)B+\gamma^{D/L}(\omega)\,\mathbf{k}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{B},
L000100	\label{sym2}
L000101	\end{equation}
L000102	with $X^{D}=-X^{L}$, where $\alpha$ describes acoustic activity, $\beta$
L000103	describes the acoustic Faraday effect and $\gamma$ describes the \textit{
L000104	polarization-independent} acoustic magneto-chiral anisotropy (aMChA). For
L000105	longitudinal modes, the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ terms are non-existent, but
L000106	this is not the case for the $\gamma$ term. Note that this argument does not
L000107	explicitly invoke chiral phonons, but the characteristic of $\alpha\neq 0$
L000108	results from the existence of non-degenerate chiral transverse phonons. The
L000109	symmetry argument does not give an indication of the strength for aMChA. For
L000110	that, we will estimate a value for $\gamma$ with a simple macroscopic
L000111	Becquerel-type model \cite{Sup-mat}: In this model, the apparent frequency
L000112	that the moving charges experience because of the magnetic field is found to
L000113	be shifted away from the externally imposed frequency by the Larmor
L000114	frequency $\Omega_{L}=qB/(2m)$, where $q$ is the charge and $m$ the mass of
L000115	the charge, the direction of the shift depending on whether the cyclotron
L000116	rotation has the same sense as the circular polarization of the incident
L000117	wave, or the opposite one. We will therefore approximate the effect of the
L000118	magnetic field on the transverse wave velocity in a chiral medium as a
L000119	frequency shift by an effective Larmor frequency $\widetilde{\Omega}
L000120	_{L}\equiv \widetilde{q}/(2\widetilde{m})$. This leads to \cite{Sup-mat}
L000121	\begin{widetext}
L000122	\begin{equation}
L000123	v_{\pm}^{D/L}(\omega,k,B) \simeq v(\omega \pm \tilde{\Omega}_L)
L000124	 \pm \alpha^{D/L}(\omega \pm \tilde{\Omega}_L) k
L000125	 \simeq v(\omega)
L000126	 \pm \alpha^{D/L}(\omega) k
L000127	 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\tilde{q}}{\tilde{m}} \frac{\partial v}{\partial \omega} B
L000128	 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\tilde{q}}{\tilde{m}} \frac{\partial \alpha^{D/L}}{\partial \omega} B k.
L000129	 \label{Chiral Becquerel}
L000130	\end{equation}
L000131	\end{widetext}
L000132	
L000133	where the third term on the right-hand side describes the acoustic Faraday
L000134	effect and the fourth term describes the aMChA. Comparing Eq.~\eqref{sym2}
L000135	with Eq.~\eqref{Chiral Becquerel} provides estimates for the $\beta$ and $
L000136	\gamma$ parameters in Eq.~\eqref{sym2}, where $\widetilde{q}$ and $
L000137	\widetilde{m}$ are effective values representing the moving charges.
L000138	
L000139	Acoustic activity theory usually limits itself to first-order spatial
L000140	dispersion, yielding an $\alpha$ independent of the wave vector \cite
L000141	{Portigal-Burstein}. This agrees well with most experimental results for
L000142	small wave vectors \cite{Shen}, but both theory and experiment acknowledge
L000143	the existence of second-order spatial dispersion contributions, i.e. $
L000144	\alpha(\omega)=\alpha_{0}+\sigma k$ \cite{Shen}. The
L000145	polarization-independent aMChA can therefore be expressed as
L000146	\begin{equation}
L000147	\frac{\Delta v}{v_{0}}\equiv \frac{v(B)-v(-B)}{v_{0}}=\frac{\widetilde{q}
L000148	\,\sigma\,\omega\, B}{\widetilde{m}\,v_{0}^{3}}.  \label{deltav/v}
L000149	\end{equation}
L000150	Note that the predicted linear frequency dependence of aMChA for this case
L000151	is different from the cubic frequency dependence predicted and observed for
L000152	the magnon-phonon hybridization case \cite{USMChA1,USMChA2}. No explicit
L000153	theory for $\sigma$ has been put forward so far, but its value can be
L000154	empirically determined from literature values of the acoustic activity of $
L000155	\alpha$-quartz at different frequencies, as summarized below:
L000156	
L000157	\begin{center}
L000158	\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
L000159	\hline
L000160	Frequency (GHz) & $\Delta v/(v f)\times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$ &
L000161	Reference \\ \hline
L000162	1.4 & 2.7 & \cite{Pine} \\
L000163	9.4 & 3.0 & \cite{Joffrin} \\
L000164	9.4 & 2.8 & \cite{Bialas} \\
L000165	28.9 & 3.3 & \cite{Pine} \\ \hline
L000166	\end{tabular}
L000167	\end{center}
L000168	
L000169	From this, we find $\sigma = (2.5 \pm 1)\times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{
L000170	m^{3}\,s^{-1}}$ \cite{Sup-mat}.
L000171	
L000172	In contrast to oMChA, in the case of aMChA, the magnetic field acts, through
L000173	the Lorentz force, both on the nuclear movement and on the bound electrons,
L000174	and both act upon each other. It is therefore not obvious what value for $
L000175	\widetilde{q}/\widetilde{m}$ to use in Eq.~\eqref{deltav/v}. It will be some
L000176	effective value between that of an electron ($1.7\times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{
L000177	C\,kg^{-1}}$) and that of nuclei ($\sim 5\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$
L000178	). It does seem very plausible that it will be the same value as in the
L000179	acoustic Faraday effect, as described by the third term in Eq.~\eqref{Chiral
L000180	Becquerel}. This value can be estimated by the following argument: In the
L000181	absence of chirality and magnetic field, the phonon dispersion relation is
L000182	given by
L000183	\begin{equation}
L000184	\omega = v_{0}k - \zeta k^{3}
L000185	\end{equation}
L000186	and therefore
L000187	
L000188	\begin{equation}
L000189	\frac{\partial v}{\partial \omega }=-\frac{6\zeta \omega }{v_{0}^{2}}.
L000190	\label{dvdw}
L000191	\end{equation}
L000192	Comparing Eq.~\eqref{sym2} with Eq.~\eqref{Chiral Becquerel} and expressing $
L000193	\beta $ in the acoustic Verdet constant $V$ \cite{Sup-mat} gives
L000194	\begin{equation}
L000195	\beta =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\widetilde{q}}{\widetilde{m}}\frac{\partial v}{
L000196	\partial \omega }=-\frac{v_{0}^{2}V}{2\omega },  \label{beta as dvdw}
L000197	\end{equation}
L000198	and upon combining Eqs.~\eqref{dvdw} and \eqref{beta as dvdw} we obtain
L000199	\begin{equation}
L000200	\frac{\widetilde{q}}{\widetilde{m}}=\frac{Vv_{0}^{4}}{6\zeta \omega ^{2}}.
L000201	\end{equation}
L000202	
L000203	Using the experimental value for $V$ at \SI{254}{MHz}, $(32\pm3)
L000204	\times10^{-3}~\mathrm{rad\ T^{-1} m^{-1}}$ \cite{Sup-mat}, and the
L000205	experimental literature value for $\zeta$, $(2.1\pm0.2)\times 10^{-16}\,
L000206	\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-1}}$ \cite{Joffrin1980}, we find $\widetilde{q}/
L000207	\widetilde{m}=(4.1\pm0.6)\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$. This value,
L000208	intermediate between the nuclear and the electronic limits, but closer to
L000209	the latter, reveals that there is indeed a significant electronic
L000210	contribution to the acoustic Faraday effect in $\alpha$-quartz. With Eq.~
L000211	\eqref{deltav/v} this yields $\Delta v/v_{0}\sim1\times 10^{-6}$ at \SI{1}{T}
L000212	and \SI{1}{GHz}. Note that this value is similar to the one predicted for
L000213	chiral Weyl semimetals \cite{Phonon-MChA-Weyl}.
L000214	
L000215	So far our argument has been limited to transverse phonons. For atoms
L000216	arranged on a helicoidal structure like in $\alpha$-quartz, the transverse
L000217	and longitudinal movements of atoms are coupled. Indeed, detailed phonon
L000218	dispersion relation calculations \cite{Chiral-phonon-database} show that
L000219	longitudinal modes in chiral crystals have some helicity and are therefore
L000220	chiral and no longer purely longitudinal. So also for longitudinal phonons,
L000221	the cyclotron motion will couple to the lattice vibrations. Also, the theory
L000222	for chiral Weyl semimetals predicts aMChA for longitudinal phonons \cite
L000223	{Phonon-MChA-Weyl}. Although not strictly justified, we will assume that Eq.~
L000224	\eqref{deltav/v} is also valid for longitudinal phonons, where $\zeta =
L000225	(7.75\pm0.05)\times 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-1}}$ \cite{Hao}. Eq.~
L000226	\eqref{deltav/v}, using the same effective value for $\widetilde{q}/
L000227	\widetilde{m}$, predicts for this case $\Delta v/v_{0}\sim2\times 10^{-7}$
L000228	at \SI{1}{T} and \SI{1}{GHz}.
L000229	
L000230	To observe such small non-reciprocities, we have designed and constructed a
L000231	dedicated ultrasound setup, as schematically shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:schema}
L000232	and described in detail in the Supplementary Information. The
L000233	improved sensitivity of this setup as compared to existing techniques
L000234	results from (i) the use of an interferometer, which doubles the aMChA
L000235	response whereas at the same time it suppresses common mode artefacts (ii) the use of an alternating magnetic field and phase sensitive detection of
L000236	the interferometer output on the magnetic field frequency.
L000237	\begin{figure}[t]
L000238	\centering  \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{schema.png}
L000239	\caption{Schematic view of the ultrasound interferometer. RF switches S1, S2
L000240	and S3 direct RF excitation pulses towards the ZnO transducers T1 and T2, or
L000241	the transmitted signals from the transducers to a differential amplifier
L000242	(the situation shown).}
L000243	\label{fig:schema}
L000244	\end{figure}
L000245	
L000246	Transverse or longitudinal short ultrasound pulses with mW power are
L000247	simultaneously injected with piezoelectric ZnO transducers sputtered on both
L000248	ends of  $z$-cut $\alpha $-quartz crystals (typical length \SI{10}{mm})
L000249	aligned parallel to the external magnetic field. The difference between the
L000250	two transmitted counterpropagating pulses, proportional to the
L000251	non-reciprocity, is then down-converted and the resulting signal is
L000252	phase-sensitively detected. This results in a typical experimental
L000253	resolution of $\Delta v/v_{0}\sim 10^{-8}$ at \SI{500}{MHz} and \SI{1}{T},
L000254	two orders of magnitude better than that in Refs.~\cite{USMChA1,USMChA2},
L000255	and sufficient to observe the predicted aMChA in $\alpha $-quartz. aMChA
L000256	measurements were performed at room temperature on several samples cut from
L000257	natural $\alpha $-quartz crystals, the handedness of which was determined
L000258	from the sign of their optical rotation.
L000259	
L000260	\begin{figure}[t]
L000261	\centering  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{dv_over_v_vs_b.png}
L000262	\caption{aMChA for longitudinal (blue) and transverse (red) waves in L
L000263	(full) and D (open) $\protect\alpha$-quartz crystals. Symbols: circles
L000264	(L-long, 481~MHz), squares (L-trans, 352~MHz), triangles (D-long, 340~MHz),
L000265	and pentagons (D-trans, 325~MHz). Solid lines are linear fits. Vertical bars
L000266	indicate typical uncertainties.}
L000267	\label{fig:dv_over_v_vs_b}
L000268	\end{figure}
L000269	
L000270	Figure~\ref{fig:dv_over_v_vs_b} shows the results for $\Delta v/v_{0}$ as a
L000271	function of the magnetic field amplitude, for longitudinal and linearly
L000272	polarized transverse waves, obtained for a $D$ and an $L$ crystal, clearly
L000273	showing a linear magnetic-field dependence and opposite signs for the two
L000274	handednesses, both defining characteristics of MChA. Figure~\ref
L000275	{fig:dv_over_v_vs_f} shows the results for $\left|\Delta v/v_{0}\right|/B$
L000276	as a function of the ultrasound frequency, for longitudinal and transverse
L000277	waves respectively. The linear frequency dependence predicted by our simple
L000278	model is clearly confirmed.
L000279	
L000280	\begin{figure}[tbp]
L000281	\centering  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{dv_over_v_vs_f.pdf}
L000282	\caption{Frequency dependence of the aMChA field slope for longitudinal
L000283	(blue) and transverse (red) waves in L (full) and D (open) $\protect\alpha$
L000284	-quartz crystals. Symbols: circles (L-long), triangles (D-long), and
L000285	pentagons (D-trans). Solid lines are linear fits to the longitudinal and
L000286	transverse datasets. Vertical bars indicate typical uncertainties. }
L000287	\label{fig:dv_over_v_vs_f}
L000288	\end{figure}
L000289	
L000290	The experimentally observed slope for longitudinal waves is $(20\pm3)\times
L000291	10^{-8}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1}$ at \SI{340}{MHz}. The prediction for this mode at
L000292	this frequency is $(8\pm3)\times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1}$. The
L000293	experimentally observed slope for transverse waves at \SI{352}{MHz} is $
L000294	(72\pm8)\times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1}$. The prediction for this mode at
L000295	this frequency is $(23\pm10)\times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1}$. In view of the
L000296	approximations in the Becquerel-like model, the agreement of its predictions
L000297	with experiment is quite satisfactory. The only experimental observation
L000298	that is not reproduced by the model is the opposite sign of aMChA for
L000299	longitudinal and transverse waves for a given crystal handedness. This
L000300	discrepancy may result from our assumption that Eq.~\eqref{deltav/v},
L000301	derived for transverse waves, is also valid for longitudinal waves. Better
L000302	agreement can be expected from detailed lattice dynamics calculations
L000303	including an external magnetic field, something that does not yet seem to
L000304	exist.
L000305	
L000306	The equivalent measurement of oMChA has also been reported for $\alpha$
L000307	-quartz, yielding $(\Delta v/v_{0})/B = 6\times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{T}^{-1}$ at
L000308	an optical wavelength of \SI{632}{nm} \cite{Kalugin}, i.e. three orders of
L000309	magnitude weaker than aMChA at the same wavelength.
L000310	
L000311	As no specific characteristics of $\alpha$-quartz, other than the values of
L000312	some general parameters, enter our model, one can safely assume that all
L000313	diamagnetic chiral crystals will possess aMChA. This in turn implies that
L000314	also the thermal conductivity of all dielectric chiral crystals will show
L000315	MChA, at least at low temperatures where acoustic phonons dominate the heat
L000316	transport. Our model provides guidelines for what parameters of chiral
L000317	diamagnetic crystals could lead to significant aMChA. Unfortunately, only
L000318	very few experimental data exist on the dispersion of acoustic activity or
L000319	on the acoustic Faraday effect in diamagnetic crystals, and, to our
L000320	knowledge, none are currently available on other chiral diamagnetic crystals.
L000321	
L000322	A special case consists of diamagnetic crystals of chiral molecules, where
L000323	the lattice building blocks themselves can also have electronic and
L000324	vibrational chirality, which can couple to ultrasound propagation. It is
L000325	unclear whether our macroscopic model can provide a good description of this
L000326	case. The observation of aMChA for longitudinal waves in crystals suggests
L000327	that aMChA could also exist for sound propagation in chiral gases and
L000328	liquids, and in their thermal conductivity. Our model does most likely not
L000329	apply to such media. It will also not apply to paramagnetic crystals, but we
L000330	do expect a significant aMChA to exist for those too. The observation of
L000331	aMChA in diamagnetic crystals implies also the existence of the inverse
L000332	effect in such crystals, the generation of a longitudinal magnetization when
L000333	unpolarized acoustic waves, or a heat flux, traverse a chiral crystal, the
L000334	sign of which depends on the handedness of the crystal.
L000335	
L000336	In conclusion, we have observed for the first time acoustic magneto-chiral
L000337	anisotropy in a diamagnetic crystal, and have developed a simple
L000338	macroscopic, Becquerel-type, model to describe our observations. This result
L000339	opens a huge class of materials (see e.g. \cite{Chiral-phonon-database} for
L000340	inorganic chiral crystals and \cite{Rekis} for molecular chiral crystals)
L000341	for the study of aMChA and its possible applications in phononics.
